Title: Project Gutenberg treats public-domain works as freely usable but protects its name and redistribution terms
Description: Project Gutenberg makes the Gettysburg Address (and other U.S. public-domain works) available for free, but its Full Project Gutenberg License imposes requirements for redistribution tied to the Project Gutenberg trademark and distribution practices — creating obligations for anyone who redistributes Gutenberg-marked files even when the underlying work is public domain.
Audience: Digital librarians, educators, volunteer transcribers, small publishers and platforms that redistribute public-domain texts
Rationale: This is the clearest, concrete tension in the source: the text is explicitly public domain in the U.S., yet Gutenberg’s license and trademark rules require redistributors to follow specific terms (for example, keeping the full license and a required sentence about Project Gutenberg, or meeting payment/royalty rules if charging). That fact is tightly supported by quoted license sections and is immediately relevant to anyone who wants to reuse or republish Gutenberg eBooks without legal missteps. Important uncertainties (how trademark enforcement is applied in practice, or international legal variations) are present in the source and should be flagged when developing the piece.
Evidence: Explicit statements: “Creating the works from print editions not protected by U.S. copyright law means that no one owns a United States copyright in these works… you can copy and distribute it in the United States without permission” (pg4.md). License requirements: Section 1.E.1 mandates a specific sentence with links be included whenever a Project Gutenberg work is distributed; 1.E.4–1.E.7 forbid removing the full license and set redistribution format requirements; 1.B and 1.E.8 describe Project Gutenberg as a registered trademark with special rules (including a 20% royalty clause if you charge for access to Project Gutenberg works). The license repeatedly distinguishes the public-domain status of the underlying text from the Foundation’s terms for distributing works “with the phrase ‘Project Gutenberg’ associated with” them.
